name: Dilemmas and Two-Way Attacks
keyCorrections: If the opponent defends both attacks easily: your dilemma is not connected — the two threats must share a structural link (e.g., both attack the same arm, or both exploit the same weight distribution)
If you transition from attack A to attack B but lose position: you are committing too fully to A — keep 20% awareness on the positional outcome even while attacking
If you freeze when the opponent defends A: drill the transition from A to B until it is automatic — hesitation kills the dilemma
description: Create two threats so the opponent must defend one line and expose the other. A dilemma forces the opponent to choose between two bad options — your job is to present the choice and capitalize on either response.
shortInstruction: Link two complementary attacks so that defending one opens the other. If they block the sweep, take the submission. If they block the submission, complete the sweep.
summary: A dilemma is any position where the opponent's defensive response to one attack opens a second, equally dangerous attack. The most powerful dilemmas link a sweep and a submission (e.g., scissor sweep → kimura from closed guard) or a pass and a back take (e.g., passing to one side exposes the back). The system teaches you to chain attacks rather than firing single techniques and restarting on failure.
whyItWorks: The human brain is limited to processing one major threat at a time — a true dilemma splits their attention and guarantees a reaction lag
Linking attacks creates compounding pressure — even if they defend the first attack perfectly, they arrive in a worse position than where they started
Two-way attacks exploit the opponent's defensive instincts — their trained reaction to one threat becomes the opening for the second
The highest-level grapplers (Danaher, Gordon Ryan) build their entire game around dilemmas rather than individual techniques
commonMistakes: Committing 100% to one attack and having no plan B when it fails
Chaining attacks that are unrelated — the second attack must be a natural consequence of defending the first
Moving too fast through the sequence — each attack must be a genuine threat, not just a transition motion
Not recognizing when the opponent has neutralized both threats — this is the time to reset, not force a third low-probability attack
coachingCues: Two threats, one choice for them
If they stop A, give them B
Every attack sets up the next
safetySummary: Do not force a dilemma at high speed — chain attacks at controlled pace to prevent accidental joint trauma
When attacking with a two-way submission chain (e.g., armbar to triangle), apply submissions progressively, not explosively
Be aware that training partners may tap to the threat of a submission rather than the actual pressure — respect the early tap

systemLogic.corePrinciple: A dilemma requires three components: (1) a connected pair of attacks, (2) shared structural mechanics, and (3) a recognition trigger to switch between them

decisionTree.action: A dilemma requires three components: (1) a connected pair of attacks, (2) shared structural mechanics, and (3) a recognition trigger to switch between them
the two attacks must target different parts of the opponent's body or different defensive responses. Examples: sweep + submission, choke + armbar, pass + back take
both attacks must flow from the same structural position. If you have to change your entire body position to switch attacks, it is not a dilemma — it is two separate techniques
you must know exactly when to switch. The trigger is almost always the same: the moment they commit their weight or hands to defend A, you transition to B

Closed guard: scissor sweep (they post hand → kimura) or armbar (they posture → triangle). Mount: armbar (they defend arm → cross choke) or cross choke (they defend neck → armbar). Back: rear-naked choke (they defend neck → bow-and-arrow) or bow-and-arrow (they defend hip → RNC). Leg locks: heel hook (they defend inside → outside ashi) or straight ankle lock (they defend heel hook → ankle lock)

moneyDetails: Dilemmas are the primary scoring mechanism in high-level BJJ — the majority of points and submissions come from two-way attacks, not single techniques
A single well-constructed dilemma can finish a match in seconds by creating an unsolvable problem for the opponent
Building a game around dilemmas rather than individual techniques is the fastest path to advanced level BJJ
The best grapplers in the world (Gordon Ryan, Mica Galvao, Tainan Dalpra) base their entire game on 3-4 high-percentage dilemmas
fixItFast: If your dilemma is not working: check that the two attacks share the same structural position. If you have to move significantly between them, it is not a dilemma
If the opponent is defending both attacks: add a third layer. A three-attack chain from one position is almost impossible to defend
If you keep losing position during the transition: slow down. The dilemma requires each attack to be a genuine threat — rushing makes neither attack dangerous
